passage: Swati, you're sulking over that one comment from your art teacher? Sit with your Yogesh Nana. When I was nine, in a small school in Jhansi, my report card came home with ten remarks from ten teachers. Nine said things like "bright", "helpful", "lovely handwriting". One, from the drawing master, said "careless with colours". Do you know which one I remember, seventy years later? "Careless with colours." I didn't show Amma the card for two days. I hid it under my mattress. When she finally read it, she read all nine good ones out loud to me, twice. I still remember the bad one best. But now I know it was one out of ten.

qa.q: How many remarks were on Nana's report card?
qa.a: Ten remarks from ten teachers.

qa.q: Why did Nana hide the report card under his mattress?
qa.a: The one remark, 'careless with colours', hurt so much that it seemed to be what the whole card said, so he felt ashamed to show it.

qa.q: What did Nana's Amma do that helped, and what could Swati try?
qa.a: She read all nine good remarks out loud twice; Swati could read all her own comments, count the kind ones, and see the unkind one as one of many.

qa.q: What would change if Nana had shown the card on the first day?
qa.a: Amma could have read out the good remarks sooner, and he might not have spent two days feeling ashamed.

grounding: It shows a child dwelling on one unkind school remark while nine good comments fade.

Rain hammered the tin roof of the school in Aizawl, and the bus was stuck behind a landslide, so Lalremsiami had to wait in the classroom for an hour. She opened the envelope from the class "kind words" activity. Ten slips. Nine said things like "You always share your tiffin" and "You help me with maths". One, in pencil, said, "You talk too much."
By the time her cousin Damini came with an umbrella, Lalremsiami had folded that one slip into a tiny square and was turning it over and over.
"What's that?"
"Someone thinks I talk too much."
"And the other nine?"
"I don't remember," she said, and she truly didn't.

qa.q: How many slips were in the envelope?
qa.a: Ten slips.

qa.q: Why can't Lalremsiami remember the nine kind slips?
qa.a: The one unkind slip stung and grabbed all her attention, so it felt like the real message while the kind ones faded.

qa.q: How could Damini help Lalremsiami on the walk home?
qa.a: Damini could read the nine kind slips aloud with her, and suggest keeping them somewhere she can see them.

qa.q: If you were a classmate who wrote a kind slip, what would you want Lalremsiami to know?
qa.a: That the kind words were meant, and one pencil note is not what the whole class thinks. 🤍

grounding: It shows a child, stuck waiting in the rain, dwelling on one unkind note and forgetting nine kind ones.

On the auto ride back from the parent-teacher meeting in Lajpat Nagar, Mummy was beaming. "Your class teacher said you're kind, you read well, you help the new girl, you ask good questions..."
Avni wasn't listening. She was staring at the traffic. "She said I'm messy."
"She said your desk could be tidier. Once."
At home, Avni's big sister Kashish asked, "How did it go?"
"Ma'am thinks I'm messy," Avni said, and went to her room.
Mummy looked at Kashish and sighed. "Nine good things, and that's all she heard."
Later Kashish knocked on Avni's door with a notebook. "Tell me the nine," she said. "I'll write them down."

qa.q: What did the class teacher say about Avni's desk?
qa.a: That her desk could be tidier, once.

qa.q: Why is Avni fixed on the word 'messy'?
qa.a: The one criticism felt sharp and personal, so it drowned out the kind, helpful, good-reader comments Mummy was so happy about.

qa.q: Why might Kashish's notebook idea help?
qa.a: Writing down all nine good things gives them a place to stay, so Avni can look at them next to the one comment.

qa.q: What is the meeting like from Mummy's side?
qa.a: Mummy came out proud and beaming, and it deflates her to see Avni hear only the one comment.

grounding: It shows a child hearing many good comments at a school meeting but holding on to one critical remark.

"Mehak, why aren't you eating? You won second place!"
"Sonali didi, look at this." Mehak pushed the science fair notebook across the table. "Someone wrote 'messy handwriting, hard to read.'"
Sonali flipped through it. "Mehak. There are ten comments here. 'Great model!' 'Very clear explanation.' 'I learned about rainwater harvesting.' 'Best volcano ever' — okay, that one's confused, but still."
"But the messy one."
"That's one. Nine people loved it."
"The judge might have been the one who wrote it."

Sonali sighed and read the good ones out loud, slowly, one by one. Mehak didn't look up.

passage:
I'm Pema. In Class 4 our teacher made us swap story notebooks and write one line about each other's story.
My story was about a yak who wanted to fly. Eight people wrote nice things. "Funny." "I liked the yak's name." "Can you write part 2?" But Varun wrote: "Boring ending."
I read Varun's line maybe fifty times. I didn't even remember the nice ones until Amala asked me about part 2 a week later. For days I thought my story was bad, and I stopped writing in my free period.
Now I think it was just one line. Eight people liked it. Varun doesn't even like yaks.
I finished part 2 in Class 5. The yak flies.

qa.q: What did Varun write about Pema's story?
qa.a: "Boring ending."

qa.q: Why did Pema read Varun's line so many times?
qa.a: The one unkind line hurt and felt more important than the nice ones, so it kept pulling Pema's attention back and made the whole story seem bad.

qa.q: What was the turning point that helped Pema, and why?
qa.a: Amala asking about part 2 reminded Pema of the eight kind comments, which helped Pema see the one line as just one opinion.

qa.q: How might Varun feel on learning how long Pema thought about that line?
qa.a: Varun might be surprised, since Varun probably wrote it quickly without thinking it would stop Pema from writing.

grounding: It shows a child forgetting eight good comments and dwelling on one unkind remark about a school story.

passage: In Class 5 our teacher had everyone write one kind thing about each classmate on little cards. I'm Jaya, and I got twenty-two cards. Twenty-one were nice: "Jaya draws the best horses," "Jaya always shares her crayons," "Jaya is funny." One, with no name on it, said: "Jaya talks too much." I read that one on the bus, at dinner and under the blanket with a torch. I didn't read the other ones again at all. The next morning I hardly spoke in class. Leela noticed and asked why. When I told her, she said, "You got twenty-one nice ones and you're sad about one?" I counted them again. She was right, but the one still felt louder.

qa.q: How many cards did Jaya get?
qa.a: Jaya got twenty-two cards.

qa.q: Why did the one unkind card feel so big to Jaya?
qa.a: Jaya felt hurt and embarrassed, and the unkind card grabbed her attention so strongly that the twenty-one kind ones faded.

qa.q: What could Jaya try when one bad comment keeps looping?
qa.a: She could read the kind cards out loud, as she did when counting again, or keep them where she can see them next to the unkind one.

qa.q: How did Leela see the pile of cards?
qa.a: Leela saw twenty-one kind cards and one unkind one, and was surprised Jaya was sad about just one.

grounding: Shows a child dwelling on one unkind remark while forgetting many kind comments from classmates.

passage:
Class 4 English, note to self, Tuesday.
I returned the story notebooks today. In Aparna's I had written nine comments: "lovely opening", "great describing words", "I laughed at the parrot" and more. At the end, one line in red: "Please check your spellings." At break, Dilnaz told me Aparna was crying in the corridor. When I found Aparna, she held out the notebook, pointing only at the red line. "You said my spellings are bad." I asked her to read me the other comments. She read them in a flat voice, as if they belonged to someone else. We made a deal: she'll circle every green comment first, then look at the red one. And I'll write my next corrections in the same colour as my praise.

qa.q: What did the one red line in Aparna's notebook say?
qa.a: It said, 'Please check your spellings.'

qa.q: Why did Aparna read the kind comments in a flat voice?
qa.a: Aparna felt hurt and ashamed about the spellings, and that one red line had grabbed all her attention, so the praise felt as if it belonged to someone else.

qa.q: What did the teacher and Aparna agree to do, and why might it help?
qa.a: Aparna will circle every green comment before looking at the red one, and the teacher will write corrections in the same colour as praise, so one remark doesn't stand out so painfully.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz have been feeling when telling the teacher?
qa.a: Dilnaz was probably worried about Aparna crying and wanted an adult to help.

grounding: Shows a child fixing on one critical remark and ignoring nine warm comments from a teacher.

passage:
Sunday
Today at the colony match I took two catches and made fourteen runs. Everybody said good things. Imran bhai said "shabash", Uncle Pinto said I field like a pro, and even the big boys clapped. But then I dropped one easy catch and Francis shouted "Butterfingers!" and some of them laughed.
Now it's night and all I can hear in my head is BUTTERFINGERS. I don't even remember exactly what Uncle Pinto said. I wanted to tell Abbu about the catches, but I told him about the drop instead.
Abbu said, "Two catches, fourteen runs, one drop. Write the numbers down." So I did. Two is more than one. I know that. It still feels like the drop was the biggest thing.
Wasim

qa.q: How many runs did Wasim make?
qa.a: Wasim made fourteen runs.

qa.q: Why does 'Butterfingers' ring in Wasim's head more than the praise?
qa.a: Wasim feels embarrassed and hurt, and the mocking word grabbed more attention than all the good things said, so it feels like the biggest part of the day.

qa.q: Why is Abbu's idea of writing the numbers down helpful?
qa.a: Seeing two catches, fourteen runs and one drop on paper puts the good and bad side by side, so the drop doesn't take over.

qa.q: How might Francis see that one shout?
qa.a: Francis might think it was just a joke in the moment, without realising it stayed with Wasim all day.

grounding: Shows a child letting one mocking shout outweigh a day of praise from others.

passage: In the village school in Barshi, the Class 5 teacher returned the story notebooks with comments. passage: At the end of term at her school in Valencia, Hana's report card came home. Her teacher had written about her reading, kindness, painting and more: nine happy lines. passage: At the art club in the community centre in Mysore, Ira ma'am looked at each clay pot. She stopped at Chaitanya's. "Lovely shape. Nice smooth sides. Good idea with the handle. Great colours." Then she tapped the rim. "This part is a bit wobbly." Chaitanya's face fell. For the rest of the class he didn't touch the clay. At pickup he told his mother, "Ira ma'am said my pot is wobbly." "Is that all she said?" "Yes." Ira ma'am heard him. She knelt down. "I said four good things first, remember? Shape, sides, handle, colours. And one small thing." Chaitanya looked at her. "You did?" "I did. The wobbly rim is the easiest bit to fix." He looked at his pot again and saw the handle he'd made.

qa.q: What did Ira ma'am say was a bit wobbly?
qa.a: The rim of the pot.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling for the rest of the class?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and hurt, focusing on the one criticism so much that he stopped working on the clay.

qa.q: How did Ira ma'am help Chaitanya see the full picture?
qa.a: She reminded him of the four good things she said first and called the wobbly rim the easiest bit to fix.

qa.q: How might Ira ma'am feel on hearing Chaitanya's report to his mother?
qa.a: She might feel surprised and a little sad that her praise was forgotten, which is why she knelt to remind him.

grounding: Shows a child dwelling on one criticism of his clay pot and forgetting four pieces of praise.

Tuesday, the week before the summer holidays. Parveen's water-cycle model stood on the front bench. Nine sticky notes from classmates covered the board beside it: Cool clouds! So neat! I want to make one! And one note, in pencil: Looks babyish.
Parveen read the nine notes once. She read the pencil one eleven times.
Thursday. At home she started painting the cotton clouds grey. "It looks babyish," she told Shalini, her older sister.
"Who said?"
"One person."
"And the others?"
Parveen shrugged. She couldn't remember what the others said.
Saturday. Shalini made her fetch the sticky notes and read them all aloud, one by one. By the ninth, Parveen was almost smiling. She put the pencil note at the bottom of the pile.

qa.a: Nine sticky notes praised Parveen's model.

qa.a: Parveen felt hurt and embarrassed, and the one unkind note grabbed her attention far more than the nine kind ones.

qa.q: What did Shalini do on Saturday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Shalini had Parveen read all the notes aloud, which brought the nine kind comments back into view.

Kamal, you're sulking over one red mark? Let me tell you about my Class 5 report card. I, Urmila, still remember it, sixty years later.
It came the week before Diwali. Nine subjects said "very good" or "excellent". And the drawing teacher had written: "Untidy. Could try harder."
I didn't light a single sparkler that Diwali. I sat on the steps with the card, reading "untidy" over and over. My mother had to pry it out of my hands.
She read me the nine good lines, one by one, and made me count them on my fingers. Then she said, "One teacher had one bad day with your drawing. Nine teachers liked you all year."
I lit my sparkler on the last night. I kept that card. I can still recite the unkind line, but now I can recite the nine too.

qa.q: What did the drawing teacher write on the card?
qa.a: The drawing teacher wrote, 'Untidy. Could try harder.'

qa.q: Why couldn't Urmila enjoy Diwali that year?
qa.a: Urmila felt hurt and ashamed, reading 'untidy' over and over, so the one unkind line outweighed nine good ones.

qa.q: Which moment in the story helped Urmila, and why?
qa.a: The mother reading the nine good lines aloud and counting them on Urmila's fingers put the one bad remark in proportion.

qa.q: How might Urmila's mother have felt that Diwali?
qa.a: The mother was probably worried and tender, seeing one line spoil the festival and gently prying the card away.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a childhood report card where one unkind remark outweighed nine good ones.

"I looked like a duck."

"I only heard the duck."

passage: On the last school day before Christmas, Leela carried her report card home through the cold Delhi fog. Nine teachers had written kind things: "excellent reader", "helpful in class", "beautiful handwriting", "asks great science questions". "It says excellent reader. It says helpful." "But it also says I talk too much." "That's one line, Leela. There are nine good ones." Leela nodded, but in bed she could still see only that one line, glowing behind her eyes in the dark.
